title: Some Prep Programs Do a Better Job of Building Teachers' Knowledge
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler reports on new NCTQ data linking first-time pass rates on elementary teacher licensure tests to specific preparation programs. Overall only 45 percent of candidates pass on the first try, far below nursing, and the gap between the best and worst programs within a state averages 56 percentage points. She presents Western Kentucky University's coursework choices and test-prep practices as one example of what seems to work, and notes states like Florida and Texas that have used the data to push for improvement. She is careful about the limits, since small samples and mixed institutional versus subgroup results can mislead. Her argument is that program-level content-knowledge data can spur improvement in one piece of a flawed system, alongside larger problems such as ed-school resistance to cognitive science and weak early-reading training.
points: Only 45 percent of candidates in states with well-structured licensure tests pass on the first attempt, compared with about 85 percent in nursing.
Linking pass rates to individual programs reveals huge within-state variation, with some institutions at under 50 percent and some far above the state average.
Western Kentucky requires targeted content coursework and uses diagnostic tests and study guides, and its candidates of color outperformed the state average.
The data must be used with care because small sample sizes and subgroup-versus-overall differences can distort the picture.
Content-knowledge pass rates address only one of many problems in teacher education, including inattention to learning science and early reading.
quotes: How many prospective elementary teachers manage to pass a test on subjects they’ll be expected to teach—required for a teaching license—on the first try? And which teacher prep programs provided their training?

The data show that overall, only 45% of candidates in states that have a “well-structured licensure test” pass on their first attempt. By “well-structured,” NCTQ means that candidates are tested separately on different content areas, so that a high score in, say, English language arts isn’t allowed to make up for a low score in math. The overall pass rate has been public for at least a couple of years now, and it compares unfavorably with other fields. In nursing, for example, the first-time pass rate averages about 85%.
One key question is why teacher candidates at some programs do much better than those at others: there’s an average 56 percentage-point difference

Still, the data needs to be used with care. While candidates of color did better than the state average at Western Kentucky, the overall pass rate for the institution was actually lower: 41% as compared to 46%. And some schools where candidates of color did well had few such students; a pass rate of 100% doesn’t mean much when it’s based on one test-taker.

More fundamentally, the failure to ensure that prospective elementary teachers have adequate content knowledge is only one of many problems with teacher education. Ed school faculty are generally unaware of or hostile to the body of scientific evidence on how people learn, and candidates are routinely encouraged to use techniques that contradict it. And many prep programs provide inadequate training in early reading skills.

But pass rates on content knowledge tests, tied to specific institutions, can serve as an impetus to improving at least one part of a seriously flawed system. NCTQ’s evidence suggests that if programs identify gaps in candidates’ content knowledge early and take steps to address them, they can help ensure that those charged with teaching children about social studies, math, science, and English language arts will have a grounding in those areas. That doesn’t seem like too much to ask for.
